results.title: (PDF) Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning with Differential Privacy
results.content: Poisoning attacks involve malicious clients manipulating their local training data or model updates to corrupt the global model.6 These attacks can degrade the global model's performance, introduce backdoors, or cause it to behave maliciously.6 FL is inherently susceptible to poisoning attacks because the decentralized structure means the central server does not have direct access to raw data, making it difficult to verify the authenticity of local updates.75 DP can be used as a defense against poisoning attacks by adding noise to updates, making it harder for malicious contributions to stand out.74 However, DP's effectiveness against poisoning The unremovable noise introduced by DP can significantly af fect model accuracy.76 Moreover, simultaneously addressing both privacy and robustness against poisoning is challenging; secure aggregation protocols (often used with DP) can obscure local updates, inadvertently facilitating poisoning attacks by preventing anomaly detection techniques from accessing unencrypted data.77 Some studies indicate that even with DP, plaintext transmission of intermediate content can lead to privacy leakage, making the system vulnerable to internal and Backdoor attacks are a type of poisoning attack where malicious participants introduce hidden triggers into their local models that, when aggregated, implant malicious behaviors into the global model.78 The global model then behaves normally on untampered data but misclassifies inputs containing the specific trigger.78 These attacks pose a serious threat to FL systems, as they can be stealthy and effective even with partial adversarial participation.80 DP defenses have demonstrated effectiveness against backdoor attacks in FL, for instance, by clipping the norm of model updates and adding Gaussian noise.78 However, a significant limitation is that existing DP defenses often incur a substantial degradation in the performance of the aggregated models on benign tasks.79 A direct implementation of DP methods introduces a trade-off between privacy preservation and model performance.81 This has led to novel two-stage approaches that first identify and exclude malicious model updates (e.g., by leveraging out-of-distribution characteristics of backdoor samples) before applying DP.

results.title: Privacy by Design: Practical Challenges and Solutions in Federated Learning for Industry | by Ayush Kumar | Medium
results.content:
Title: Privacy by Design: Practical Challenges and Solutions in Federated Learning for Industry | by Ayush Kumar | Medium
# Privacy by Design: Practical Challenges and Solutions in Federated Learning for Industry. That combination of disciplines is what I mean by privacy-by-design, and it is what I will outline for teams trying to move federated learning, or FL, from prototype to production. Federated learning is a collaboration pattern in which many clients (mobile devices, IoT devices, hospital servers, or partner company nodes) train a model locally on their private data, and send model updates, not raw examples, to a central coordinator that aggregates them into a global model. For FL, that means threat modeling before picking algorithms, selecting privacy-enhancing technologies, and building observability and governance into every training round. 3. Engineering complexity: FL brings distributed systems challenges (client churn and unreliable connectivity), statistical issues (non-IID data), and new attack vectors (poisoning and model inversion). Regulators tend to treat FL as a privacy enhancing technology that can reduce risk, but they still expect thorough documentation, demonstrable mitigations, and DPIAs. Multinational pilots require careful legal review and clear contracts describing responsibilities, liabilities, and permitted audit rights. Defending against these attacks typically requires anomaly detection or robust aggregation, which can conflict with privacy-preserving designs if they require per-client visibility. In FL, teams commonly use client-level DP, which bounds the influence of any single client on the global model. Practical approach: use privacy accountants to track cumulative privacy loss over rounds, and choose conservative but usable epsilon budgets based on threat modeling and stakeholder risk appetite. Client layer, the SDK on devices or partner nodes, handles local training, model versioning, compression, and local clipping or noising if DP is applied on-device. Coordination layer, the server-side orchestrator, samples clients for each active round, distributes model checkpoints and hyperparameters, coordinates key exchange for secure aggregation, and handles retries for clients that drop out or fail. Federated learning can enable powerful collaborations while respecting data minimization, but privacy-by-design requires engineering discipline, cross-team coordination, and operational maturity. The right approach is layered: combine secure aggregation with differential privacy where needed, use robust aggregation to defend against active attacks, embrace personalization to address non-IID data, and invest heavily in governance, simulators, and observability.

results.title: AI for Federated Learning and Privacy-Preserving AI: Constructing Cryptographically Secure and Statistically Robust Distributed Inference
results.content: # AI for Federated Learning and Privacy-Preserving AI: Constructing Cryptographically Secure and Statistically Robust Distributed Inference. Federated Learning (FL) introduces an inherently adversarial and heterogeneous computational environment, where model updates must be aggregated securely while ensuring privacy guarantees, statistical robustness, and resilience to adversarial interference. This article deconstructs the foundational primitives of cryptographic security in FL, explores privacy-preserving inference mechanisms, and dissects robust statistical learning frameworks that mitigate adversarial corruption and systemic biases in decentralized models. To counteract these threats, federated learning relies on homomorphic encryption (HE), zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), and threshold cryptography, ensuring that updates remain verifiable yet encrypted throughout the training lifecycle. * Lattice-Based Cryptographic Hardness: Modern homomorphic encryption (HE) schemes hinge on the complexity of the Ring Learning With Errors (RLWE) problem, a lattice-based cryptographic construct that ensures security even against quantum adversaries. * zk-SNARKs and zk-STARKs for Federated Model Integrity: Zero-Knowledge Proofs allow a client to prove that a model update was computed honestly without revealing the raw update itself. * Multiplicative Secret Sharing for Privacy-Preserving Model Training: Cryptographic protocols such as Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) enable federated clients to perform gradient aggregation in encrypted space without exposing raw model updates to any party. ### Statistical Robustness and Differential Privacy in Federated Learning. Ensuring provable privacy guarantees in federated learning requires differential privacy (DP) mechanisms that mitigate information leakage from gradient updates, preventing adversaries from reconstructing user-specific data. * RDP in Gaussian Mechanisms: Unlike Laplace mechanisms traditionally used in DP, Gaussian noise addition under RDP ensures subsampling-based privacy amplification, where model updates contribute probabilistically to the aggregated result. * Optimal Noise Distribution: The injected noise must align with the Gaussian Mechanism's privacy budget to ensure DP-compliant aggregation while preserving model utility. * Random Subsampling for Privacy Amplification: Instead of applying global noise to all updates, subsampling techniques allow model updates to be differentially private with reduced computational overhead. ### The Future of Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning. The integration of cryptographic security, differential privacy, and fairness constraints into federated learning redefines distributed AI. * ### The Future of AI, Quantum Computing, Blockchain, and Reinforcement Learning: A Comprehensive Overview with Critiques and Future Strategies. * ### Blockchain-Backed Federated Learning: A Breakthrough for AI Privacy.
